segments.title: The 1897 defeat behind Greek naval reform
segments.body: An earlier defeat by Russia had driven Ottoman military reform with German support. By 1897 the Ottoman army was larger, better organized and better supplied than its Greek opponent. Greek training and organization had barely advanced since independence, leaving the army poorly prepared for war. British and French naval intervention prevented the Ottoman victory from becoming an unrestricted defeat of Greece because the great powers would not allow either side to overwhelm the other. Ottoman court factionalism then diverted attention from further preparation, while Greece faced the need to rebuild its armed forces.

evidence.note: Ottoman reform after defeat by Russia, Greek institutional weakness in 1897, British and French intervention, and subsequent political obstacles to reform.

segments.summary: The Greek defeat of 1897 and Ottoman military modernization explain why Greece entered the next conflict determined to rebuild its armed forces.

segments.title: Admiral Tufnell's mission rebuilds the Hellenic Navy
segments.body: The British naval mission arrived in 1911, after Georgios Averof had already been ordered and launched. Lionel Tufnell brought experience from commanding a naval engineering college and received broad authority over procurement, infrastructure and training. Engineers and instructors formed the mission because Greece needed the capacity to maintain and operate its navy. His battleship proposal crossed national rivalries by combining German construction with American guns. The short interval before war left no chance of completing the proposed construction programme. Capable Greek officers and their willingness to accept outside advice were essential to the reform.

evidence.note: Tufnell's authority, mission personnel, infrastructure work, and multinational battleship proposal.

segments.summary: A British mission led by Lionel Tufnell receives unusually broad authority over Greek naval training, infrastructure, engineering, and procurement.

segments.title: Could Tufnell overrule the Hellenic king?
segments.body: The king had invited the British mission partly as a guarantee of British support. He therefore sought to avoid disputes with Tufnell over naval policy. His practice was to ask what the admiral recommended and then support it wholeheartedly. The king treated Tufnell as his chief naval adviser.

evidence.note: Tufnell's authority rested on the king's reliance on and consistent backing for his recommendations.

segments.summary: The king asked Tufnell for naval recommendations and backed them wholeheartedly, giving the British adviser considerable practical influence.
segments.question: Could Admiral Tufnell overrule the Hellenic king on naval policy?
segments.answerShort: The king's practice was to ask for Tufnell's recommendations and support them wholeheartedly, treating him as his chief naval adviser.

segments.title: Tufnell orders a Greek battleship across national rivalries
segments.body: Tufnell considered additional battleships necessary after comparing Greek and Ottoman naval strength. His 1912 order went to Germany, with 14-inch guns from Bethlehem Steel and an intended speed of 23 knots. British Parsons turbines were originally intended before AEG turbines were selected. The order crossed national rivalries during the Anglo-German naval arms race. Britain had more surplus yard capacity, with Thames Ironworks then going out of business, making a lack of British yard space an unconvincing explanation. One possible British advantage was that a Greek order occupied German shipbuilding capacity while American gun purchases kept that spending outside German armament development.

evidence.note: German construction, intended Parsons machinery subsequently changed to AEG turbines, Bethlehem Steel 14-inch guns, and a planned speed of 23 knots.
Surplus British yard capacity and possible benefits from occupying German construction capacity while buying American guns.

segments.summary: A British adviser selected German construction and American guns for Greece during the Anglo-German naval arms race.

segments.title: Tufnell builds capacity before new ships can arrive
segments.body: Tufnell's mission depended on capable Greek officers who were prepared to work with an outside adviser. After more than a decade of unsuccessful efforts to escape institutional stagnation, outside advice offered a way to undertake broader reform. His experience with British infrastructure improvements suited the immediate task of building capacity. War came too soon for a large construction programme, so docks, facilities and ammunition spaces mattered even while the fleet still lacked enough shells. Like installing a network inside a house, much of this preparation was difficult to see from outside. It gave the navy the means to expand rapidly during wartime.

evidence.note: Capable Greek officers and the need for outside advice after prolonged institutional stagnation.
Greek officers' cooperation and Tufnell's experience improving British infrastructure.
Limited time before war, the house-wiring analogy, and facilities and ammunition capacity for rapid expansion.

segments.summary: With too little time to transform the order of battle before war, Tufnell concentrated on the infrastructure and institutional capacity needed for rapid expansion.

segments.title: Did Tufnell visit the German shipyards?
segments.body: A Greek delegation toured the shipyards during the procurement process. Tufnell may have been among its members, but that identification remains uncertain. The difficulty is whether the name translated from Greek refers to Tufnell or another person.

evidence.note: Uncertainty about whether the member named in the Greek delegation account was Tufnell.

segments.summary: Tufnell's possible participation in a Greek shipyard delegation remains uncertain because the translated name does not establish his identity.
segments.question: Did Tufnell visit the German shipyards?
segments.answerShort: Possibly, but the name in the Greek delegation account may identify someone else when translated into English.

segments.title: Why Greek sea power mattered to the Balkan League
segments.body: Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro cooperated because hostility to the Ottoman Empire outweighed their mutual distrust. Their quarrel over the rewards of victory then led to the Second Balkan War. Greece's contribution combined land forces with a fleet able to prevent Ottoman reinforcement through the Aegean. During negotiations, the Greek ambassador argued that Greece could contribute the equivalent of 600,000 men: 200,000 on the battlefield and another 400,000 Ottoman troops prevented from landing between Salonica and Gallipoli. This was an argument for the fleet's strategic value during alliance negotiations. Greek naval forces also captured islands using personnel and infrastructure developed through the reform programme.

evidence.note: Balkan League cooperation despite rivalries and the ensuing quarrel over the gains of victory.
The Greek ambassador's negotiating claim of 200,000 Greek troops plus 400,000 Ottoman troops denied maritime reinforcement.
The Greek navy's island campaign and the infrastructure supporting its personnel.

segments.summary: The Balkan League's armies could attack on land, but the Greek fleet was essential for blocking Ottoman reinforcement and supporting an island-hopping campaign.

segments.title: Bulgaria and Serbia mobilize societies for war
segments.body: Bulgaria mobilized roughly 600,000 men from a population of about 4.3 million, around one person in seven. Its field force included nine infantry divisions, a cavalry division and 1,116 artillery pieces. Serbia called up about 255,000 from a population just under three million and organized ten infantry divisions, two independent brigades and a cavalry division. The smaller manpower total could produce more divisions because divisional strength and organization varied. Serbia's recent wars had also given its army experienced officers and battle-hardened troops. That experience makes Austria-Hungary's expectation of an easy campaign there in 1914 difficult to understand.

evidence.note: Bulgarian and Serbian populations, mobilized manpower, formation totals, divisional differences, and Serbia's recent combat experience.

segments.summary: Bulgaria and Serbia mobilized large shares of their populations, but different divisional structures make their formation totals difficult to compare.

segments.title: Greek reform produces two offensive field armies
segments.body: Although many observers expected Greece to field only about 50,000 troops after its humiliation in 1897, the reformed state mobilized 125,000 army personnel plus 140,000 National Guard and reserves, roughly 265,000 in total. French military advice and Greek willingness to learn helped reshape the army around triangular infantry divisions. Greece organized this manpower into two field armies and went on the offensive rather than remaining the coalition's weak partner. The navy then carried the campaign outward through the capture of Aegean islands. These reforms created the combined land-and-sea capacity that made Greece strategically valuable to the Balkan League.

evidence.note: French-supported reform, triangular divisions, 125,000 army personnel plus 140,000 National Guard and reserves, two field armies, and the navy's island campaign.

segments.summary: Expected to remain the Balkan League's weak partner, Greece instead mobilized roughly 265,000 personnel and paired offensive land forces with an island-hopping navy.

segments.title: Averof's regional strength and conservative design
segments.body: Georgios Averof was probably the most capable all-round warship in the region, with useful speed, armour and a mixed battery of 9.2-inch and 7.5-inch guns. She was laid down in 1907, two years after HMS Dreadnought, and retained the Pisa-class armoured-cruiser design. Italian industry could have produced a more advanced ship by then. Averof's strength against local opponents therefore coexisted with the limitations of a conservative design.

evidence.note: Averof's regional strength, 9.2-inch and 7.5-inch batteries, construction dates and Pisa-class design, with criticism of the design's limited ambition.

segments.summary: Georgios Averof was probably the Aegean's most capable warship, yet her mixed-battery armored-cruiser design was already conservative in the post-Dreadnought world.

segments.title: Russian assistance and Montenegro's readiness for war
segments.body: Montenegro was the smallest member of the Balkan League. Russian assistance had improved its military skills, making its forces a useful contribution to the coalition. It had avoided Ottoman occupation, and the Ottomans paid it little attention. That gave Montenegro time to mobilize without Ottoman interference.

evidence.note: Montenegro's small size, Russian military assistance, and opportunity to mobilize while the Ottomans ignored it.

segments.summary: Russian assistance and time to mobilize without Ottoman interference helped prepare the Balkan League's smallest member.

segments.title: Ottoman plans without the forces to execute them
segments.body: The Ottoman Empire's nominal population of about 26 million overstated the manpower it could mobilize. Recruitment on the European side of the straits depended on a much smaller population, roughly 6.1 million people including about 2.3 million Muslims, while the authorities distrusted Orthodox Christians as conscripts. Sophisticated staff plans could not turn that theoretical strength into the expected field force. War with Italy over Libya and the Dodecanese, operations in Yemen, Young Turk turmoil, and the dismissal of 70,000 mobilized troops to save money all reduced readiness. A planned mobilization approaching 600,000 therefore produced only about 200,000 troops. The staff lacked the resources to execute its plans.

evidence.note: Nominal population and the European recruitment pool differed sharply. An intended mobilisation near 600,000 produced roughly 200,000 troops after war with Italy, distant deployments, political turmoil and cost-cutting demobilisation.

segments.summary: War with Italy, internal revolution, distant deployments, and demobilization left the Ottoman army far below its planned strength in 1912.

segments.title: Orders not to risk ships constrain Ottoman command
segments.body: At his later court-martial, the Ottoman commander produced a letter from the naval minister instructing him not to let the ships be damaged. That written constraint helps explain why preserving the fleet could override the operational need to contest the Aegean. His background is harder to assess: Dr. Clarke found little biographical information, particularly in English or Turkish, and more material in Greek. This limit on the available account prevents a detailed comparison of the two commanders' careers.

evidence.note: The minister's ship-preservation order produced at the commander's court-martial and limited biographical information located, with more material in Greek than in English or Turkish.

segments.summary: A naval-ministry order not to let the fleet be damaged helps explain Ottoman caution and complicates attempts to assign responsibility to the fleet commander alone.

segments.title: Kountouriotis accepts the risks of fighting for sea control
segments.body: Kountouriotis projected confidence before battle through signals that included a taunting offer to supply the Ottoman fleet with coal. His later defence of independent action rested on the principle that warships must accept danger and possible loss if a navy is to rule the seas. He combined that willingness to fight with seamanship and an understanding of his flagship's strengths. His later offices included naval minister, regent and president of Greece. He chose Averof as his flagship because he considered her more capable than the older coastal defence ships.

evidence.note: Kountouriotis's coal taunt, acceptance of losses when fighting for sea control, choice of flagship and later political offices.

segments.summary: Kountouriotis's signals and later defense of his conduct reveal a commander who valued initiative and accepted that fleets must be risked to command the sea.

segments.title: Kountouriotis takes command of Georgios Averof
segments.body: Kountouriotis went to Britain in June 1911 to take command of Georgios Averof after unrest among her crew. The Italian-built ship had gone there for guns and its first ammunition supply. Sailors unfamiliar with blue cheese mistook its edible mould for spoiled food, provoking unrest and the replacement of the original captain. A trusted senior officer was needed to restore discipline and train the ship's company. The incident explains the practical importance of preparing personnel for unfamiliar food and customs, comparable to American preparations for personnel travelling to Britain in World War II.

evidence.note: Kountouriotis's earlier service and appointment after the blue-cheese mutiny, including the crew's misunderstanding of edible mould and the comparison with preparing American personnel for Britain.

segments.summary: Unfamiliar British food helped provoke unrest aboard Averof, bringing Kountouriotis to Britain to restore discipline and train her crew.

segments.title: The Ottoman fleet's aging and mismatched battle line
segments.body: The former German Brandenburg-class ships retained six 11-inch guns, with two 35-calibre barrels and four 40-calibre barrels. Their roughly 16.5-knot speed left them several knots behind Averof, while their machinery and protection dated from the 1890s. Other Ottoman vessels were even less satisfactory: the reconstructed ironclad Mesudiye never received her intended 9-inch guns, while ships described as destroyers were closer to German torpedo boats. German equipment purchases and military advice show that modernisation was being attempted. Political factionalism repeatedly undermined it, with officers' connections sometimes allowing junior or inexperienced men to dominate a unit.

evidence.note: Ottoman political constraints and attempted modernisation, with the principal ships' age, speed, mixed barrel lengths and incomplete armament.

segments.summary: The Ottoman battle line combined old Brandenburg-class battleships, incomplete ironclads, and small German torpedo boats with serious speed and readiness disadvantages.

segments.title: Why a three-knot advantage can decide a gunfight
segments.body: Against the Brandenburg-class battleships' roughly 16.5 knots, Averof could make about 20 knots in normal service and theoretically 23.5. About three knots of superiority lets a commander choose the range and angle of a naval engagement. Three and a half knots is a strong margin; seven makes pursuit or escape overwhelmingly one-sided. At Elli that speed advantage gave Kountouriotis the freedom to turn a material difference into positional control.

evidence.note: Averof's practical 20 knots and theoretical 23.5 knots compared with the Brandenburgs' 16.5 knots, with about three knots identified as sufficient to choose range and engagement angle.

segments.summary: Averof's speed margin over the Brandenburg-class battleships let Kountouriotis choose the range and angle of engagement.

segments.title: Mesudiye's wooden guns expose an incomplete refit
segments.body: Mesudiye was a British-built central-battery ironclad whose survival into the Balkan Wars contrasted with the Royal Navy's disposal of her sister HMS Superb in 1906. A 1903 reconstruction added Niclausse boilers and a substantial secondary battery, but the intended pair of Vickers 9-inch guns never arrived. Wooden dummies occupied their positions instead. The ship therefore looked more complete on paper than she was in combat. She remained in service until the Royal Navy submarine B11 sank her in 1914.

evidence.note: Mesudiye's British construction, 1903 reconstruction and secondary armament, with wooden dummies standing in for the undelivered Vickers 9-inch guns.

segments.summary: The reconstructed Ottoman ironclad received new boilers and secondary weapons, but wooden dummies stood where her intended Vickers 9-inch guns should have been.

segments.title: Greek destroyers and Georgios Averof create a speed advantage
segments.body: Greek destroyers purchased from an interrupted Argentine order were larger, faster, and more heavily armed than the German-built Ottoman torpedo boats. Their 31-knot speed exceeded the Ottoman boats' roughly 26 knots, and their four 4-inch guns and six torpedo tubes gave them a clear fighting advantage. The older Hydra-class coast-defense ships remained near 17 knots, making the Greek formation highly uneven. Georgios Averof supplied the decisive margin with a 20-knot practical speed, substantial armour, and a mixed battery of 9.2-inch and 7.5-inch guns. A common battle-line speed would prevent the fastest ships from fully exploiting their advantages.

evidence.note: British-built Greek destroyers from an interrupted Argentine order made 31 knots and carried four 4-inch guns and six torpedo tubes, outmatching 26-knot Ottoman boats. Averof, originally ordered for Italy and bought by Greece in 1909, could make 20 knots and carried 9.2- and 7.5-inch guns with substantial armour.

segments.summary: Fast British-built destroyers and the armored cruiser Georgios Averof gave Greece ships designed to outpace and outfight their Ottoman counterparts.

segments.title: British-built Greek destroyers outmatch Ottoman torpedo boats
segments.body: Greece acquired four new destroyers from Cammell Laird that had originally been built for Argentina. Their 31-knot speed exceeded the German-built Ottoman boats' 26 knots, while four 4-inch guns and six torpedo tubes gave the Greek ships a heavier armament. The Ottoman boats carried three torpedo tubes and much lighter guns. This difference reflected competing design purposes: the British ships were torpedo boat destroyers intended to overpower vessels like their Ottoman opponents. The Greek ships initially combined four coal-fired boilers with one oil-fired boiler, followed by an oil-fired boiler replacement in 1925.

evidence.note: British-built destroyers ordered by Argentina became available for Greek purchase as war approached.
Purchase of four Cammell Laird destroyers, mixed coal and oil firing, and later boiler replacement.
The Greek destroyers' 31 knots, four 4-inch guns and six torpedo tubes compared with the Ottoman boats' 26 knots and lighter armament.

segments.summary: Greek purchases from an Argentine order supplied fast, heavily armed destroyers suited to defeating the smaller German-built Ottoman boats.

segments.title: Hydra-class refits improve weapons while leaving speed unchanged
segments.body: The Hydra-class ships had been ordered from France in 1885 and usually operated together. Refits improved their armour and guns, but their engines could not be upgraded, leaving their top speed at 17 knots. Even that modest speed was about half a knot above the Ottoman Brandenburg-class ships. Each Hydra-class ship carried three 10.8-inch guns, providing a substantial battery in a low-lying coastal defence vessel. Their usefulness against older opponents survived despite a speed limit that separated them from Averof.

evidence.note: The 1885 French order, armour and gun improvements without an engine upgrade, retained 17-knot speed and three 10.8-inch guns.

segments.summary: The Greek coastal defence ships retained useful heavy guns and a slight speed advantage over the Ottoman battleships, despite refits that left their original engines in place.

segments.title: Averof's purchase and the limits of comparing armour thickness
segments.body: Georgios Averof had initially been ordered for the Italian navy before being offered for sale. A bequest from the Greek businessman whose name she received supplied the down payment, allowing Greece to acquire her in 1909 before her launch in 1910. Her practical operating speed was about 20 knots, although she could reach 23.5 knots at the cost of severe vibration. Four 9.2-inch guns and eight 7.5-inch guns formed her principal batteries. Her roughly 7.9-inch midships armour was much thinner than the Brandenburgs' quoted 15.7-inch belt, but the comparison also depended on the quality of armour produced at different dates. Thickness alone did not settle the relative protection of the ships.

evidence.note: The original Italian order, sale to Greece in 1909, benefactor's bequest as the down payment, launch and naming.
Averof's practical and maximum speeds, principal gun batteries, and comparison of armour thickness with older Brandenburg armour.

segments.summary: A private bequest helped Greece acquire Averof, whose speed, guns and newer armour made her an effective opponent for older battleships.

segments.title: Tenedos gives Greece a base beside the Dardanelles
segments.body: Holding Tenedos allowed the Greek navy to watch the Dardanelles approaches and keep coal and supplies close to its fleet. The Ottoman navy faced a strategic dilemma: preserving its ships inside the straits surrendered the Aegean, while using them risked the loss of its main maritime force. The uncontested capture of the island exposed a failure to protect the fleet's route into the Aegean. A possible counterstroke was a timed night dash followed by an early attack on the Greek fleet in harbour. That remained a hypothetical opportunity requiring patience and initiative.

evidence.note: Tenedos's supply value and proximity to the Dardanelles, its uncontested capture, and a hypothetical Ottoman night attack on the Greek anchorage.

segments.summary: Greek capture of Tenedos put coal, supplies, and observation close to the Ottoman fleet's exit from the Dardanelles.

segments.title: Could the Ottoman admiral lose the war in an afternoon?
segments.body: In this interpretation, Elli and the following naval battle effectively lost the war for the Ottomans. The analogy therefore extends over two defeats, described as a couple of afternoons.

evidence.note: Agreement with the proposed comparison between losing a war and the two Ottoman naval defeats, qualified as a couple of afternoons.

segments.summary: The Ottoman defeats at Elli and the following battle prompt a comparison with losing a war in two afternoons.
segments.question: Could the Ottoman admiral lose the war in an afternoon?
segments.answerShort: Yes, in that comparison: Elli and the next naval battle effectively did so, although that took a couple of afternoons.

segments.title: Byzantium, Constantinople and Istanbul
segments.body: Byzantium was the city's Greek name until 330 AD, after which it was called Constantinople. The change to Istanbul is dated to 1930. Constantinople is therefore the historical name for the First Balkan War setting. Modern maps label the same city Istanbul, so the names refer to the same place when following the Dardanelles geography.

evidence.note: Byzantium until 330 AD, Constantinople afterward, the change to Istanbul dated to 1930, and the connection between historical and modern map names.

segments.summary: The city's successive names connect the First Balkan War's Constantinople with the Istanbul shown on modern maps.

segments.title: Why the Battle of Elli has several names
segments.body: The engagement is commonly called the Battle of Elli, but Greek and Turkish usage also associates it with Helles or Imbros. Some accounts call the result inconclusive because neither side lost a ship. The losses given are two Greeks killed, 18 Ottomans killed and 41 Ottomans wounded, with limited damage to a battleship. The Ottoman withdrawal nevertheless left the Greek fleet dominant at sea. Control of the sea provides the basis for calling it a Greek victory despite the limited material losses.

evidence.note: Alternate battle names, no ships sunk, the stated Greek and Ottoman casualties, and Greek sea control after the Ottoman withdrawal.

segments.summary: Greek and Ottoman naming conventions frame the same engagement differently, while the outcome shows why sea control matters more than ship sinkings alone.

segments.title: The fleets approach Elli with different tactical problems
segments.body: The Ottoman commanders met on 14 December and planned to fight within reach of the fortified Dardanelles approaches, where shore batteries could add to their firepower. The Greek force approached with Averof leading three Hydra-class ships and four destroyers. Ottoman destroyers went forward by divisions and increasingly acted as reconnaissance vessels. The Ottoman commander interpreted Greek movements as preparations for a submarine or torpedo attack, although the basis for that interpretation remains doubtful. He changed course, increased speed to ten knots and ordered preparations for a torpedo attack.

evidence.note: Ottoman planning under shore-battery protection, the approaching Greek formation, destroyer deployments by divisions, and course and speed changes in response to a suspected torpedo attack.

segments.summary: Ottoman plans depended on support from shore batteries, but divided destroyer movements and suspected torpedo threats complicated the response to the Greek advance.

segments.title: Commerce raiding leaves Ottoman cruisers away from Elli
segments.body: Two relatively modern Ottoman protected cruisers were away conducting commerce raids instead of reinforcing the battle fleet at Elli. Their raiding attracted warnings from Britain and France. A useful independent operation therefore weakened local concentration and risked drawing great powers into the conflict. In that scenario, the Ottomans could not count on German help or large supplies of assistance. The raiding threatened to create a larger war than the Ottoman fleet could manage.

evidence.note: Two Ottoman protected cruisers were absent on commerce-raiding duties that drew British and French warnings, creating a risk of intervention without assured German help.

segments.summary: Two useful Ottoman protected cruisers were absent on commerce-raiding duties, an operation that also risked provoking Britain and France.

segments.title: Averof hoists the Z flag and attacks independently
segments.body: Kountouriotis hoisted the Z flag for independent action and took Averof away from the slower Greek ships. At about twenty knots, the flagship used her speed, armour and firepower to cross the Ottoman formation. The range closed from roughly twelve kilometres to less than three. Separating Averof from the Hydra-class ships created an unintended pincer and alarmed the Ottoman force. Ottoman ships turned rapidly toward the Dardanelles while Averof pursued them into the range of the coastal guns. The engagement lasted less than an hour and left the Greeks in control of the field.

evidence.note: Averof's independent action at about twenty knots, the closing range, the unintended pincer, and the Ottoman withdrawal toward the Dardanelles.

segments.summary: Kountouriotis used Averof's speed to leave the slower Greek line, cross the Ottoman formation, and create an unintended pincer that drove it back into the Dardanelles.

segments.title: Why concentrated Ottoman fire struggled against Averof
segments.body: The Ottomans identified Averof as the main threat and concentrated fire on her. Her low profile and speed made the task difficult for crews unused to such a target. Kountouriotis also tried to use the gaps between Ottoman ships as protection: an overshooting shell could strike a friendly vessel and make the Ottoman crews hesitate. Such conditions separated practical firing rates from theoretical ones. Averof fired 127 shells and received four heavy hits during the engagement. An estimate of 600 to 700 rounds from fully worked-up and aimed guns illustrates the additional output that better preparation might have allowed.

evidence.note: Concentrated Ottoman fire against Averof, difficulty with her speed and low profile, and friendly-fire risk when firing through gaps between ships.
Averof fired 127 shells and took four heavy hits, compared with an estimate of 600 to 700 rounds from fully worked-up guns.

segments.summary: Averof's speed, low profile and position complicated Ottoman shooting, while her own shell expenditure shows the difference between practical and theoretical gunnery.

segments.title: How did the Ottoman fleet react to Averof's pincer?
segments.body: Averof's separation from the main Greek force created an unintended pincer. Continuing on course risked leaving the Ottoman ships between the flagship and the Hydra-class vessels. Fear of being outflanked prompted hurried turns of roughly 160 degrees and a retreat toward the Dardanelles fortresses. Averof continued firing and followed into the range of the coastal guns.

evidence.note: The tactical alternatives posed are an orderly withdrawal or panic as Averof's movement threatens a pincer.
Fear of being caught between Averof and the Hydra-class ships prompted hurried turns toward the straits while Averof pursued.

segments.summary: The threat of being caught between the two Greek groups prompted hurried Ottoman turns toward the Dardanelles.
segments.question: Did the Ottoman fleet withdraw methodically or panic when Averof's movement threatened a pincer?
segments.answerShort: The hurried turns toward the straits and the protection of the coastal forts are characterized as panic.

segments.title: Elli's effect on morale carries into Lemnos
segments.body: The immediate casualty and damage totals were modest, yet the Ottoman withdrawal left the Greek fleet dominant at sea. At Lemnos the Ottomans made a second attempt to break the Dardanelles blockade and recover their Aegean position. That defeat left one Greek sailor wounded but killed 41 Ottoman personnel, wounded 104, and damaged two battleships and an ironclad. Greek crews entered the second battle willing to act aggressively, while Ottoman commanders carried the anxiety of their earlier defeat. The second failure confirmed that the Ottoman fleet could not regain control of the Aegean.

evidence.note: Elli increased Greek confidence before Lemnos, where one Greek sailor was wounded, 41 Ottoman personnel were killed, 104 were wounded, and two battleships plus an ironclad were damaged.

segments.summary: No ships sank at Elli, but the Greek victory increased confidence before the second Ottoman attempt to break the blockade at Lemnos.

segments.title: Elli pushes the Aegean naval race toward firepower and speed
segments.body: The naval rivalry continued after the Balkan Wars. Greek procurement looked to Germany and Ottoman procurement to Britain. Ottoman priorities emphasized firepower suited to fighting in the confined Aegean. The short distances there could move an encounter through several engagement ranges within minutes. Greece valued the power of the American Mississippi-class ships it bought, but found them slow beside Averof. The flagship's success had made high speed an attractive feature in later Greek naval choices.

evidence.note: Foreign battleship orders and Ottoman emphasis on firepower for the confined Aegean.
Continued naval rivalry, the power of the American Mississippi-class ships, and the Greek preference for Averof's speed.

segments.summary: Ottoman procurement emphasized firepower for the Aegean, while Greek experience with Averof encouraged a lasting preference for speed.

segments.title: What supports claims of a Greek battlecruiser programme?
segments.body: Claims of Greek battlecruiser plans include buying British ships after the Balkan Wars, acquiring surplus British battlecruisers after World War I, and joining a Dutch procurement effort. Dr. Clarke has heard these claims but has not seen supporting evidence himself. His doubts draw on familiarity with the Cammell Laird and Vickers archives, where he has not encountered papers for a Greek battlecruiser programme. He also acknowledges that he lacks comparable familiarity with Ottoman or Turkish archives. A programme could have bypassed the two British firms, but excluding major potential bidders would have been unusual given normal tendering practice. The claims remain doubtful within the limits of that personal archival experience.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke's personal account of Greek battlecruiser claims, papers not encountered at Cammell Laird or Vickers, and the limits of his archival familiarity.

segments.summary: Several Greek battlecruiser proposals are alleged, but the supporting evidence remains uncertain and the archival objection rests on a personal research account.

segments.title: Elli shows why ships alone do not make a fleet
segments.body: The Ottoman pre-dreadnoughts had enough protection and firepower to contest Averof on paper, but weak training and constrained command prevented them from using that potential. Greece won through initiative but also exposed a structural weakness: Averof was a one-off fast ship unsupported by comparable partners. Both navies needed more cruisers and destroyers, and Greece would have benefited from additional ships able to maneuver with its flagship. Two or three ships able to operate with Averof could have changed the Ottoman decision to sortie or encouraged the purchase of additional Brandenburg-class battleships. The victory therefore demonstrates both the value of aggressive command and the danger of making a fleet depend on one exceptional ship.

evidence.note: Ottoman training and command restrictions limited the use of their battleships, while both fleets lacked sufficient supporting cruisers and destroyers. Additional ships like Averof could have changed Ottoman choices.

segments.summary: The battle's main lesson is that training, command freedom, and a balanced force mattered as much as nominal armor and gun power.

segments.title: Could Greece and the Ottoman Empire afford balanced fleets?
segments.body: Ottoman corruption diverted resources that could have supported a more effective fleet. Greece was building a maritime economy but still lacked infrastructure and kept tight control of naval spending. Buying ships one at a time reduced the scale of its commitments, and Averof had been acquired while already under construction in Italy. Further purchases could have come from foreign yards building vessels for customers who no longer wanted to complete them. Both states possessed resources, but their institutions and spending choices restricted what reached the fleet.

evidence.note: Affordability of balanced fleets, Ottoman corruption, Greek financial caution and infrastructure limits, and purchases of foreign ships already under construction.

segments.summary: Money existed, but Ottoman corruption and Greek reluctance to commit funds constrained balanced fleet construction.
segments.question: Could Greece and the Ottoman Empire afford to build more balanced fleets?
segments.answerShort: Yes, but Ottoman corruption and Greek caution over spending and infrastructure limited what each navy could turn into an effective force.

segments.title: What if Greece had ordered a battleship from America?
segments.body: An American battleship order is proposed alongside the Greek purchase of Salamis from Germany. Exchange rates raise the possibility that American construction could have been similarly affordable. The German order also offered a diplomatic attraction by making Greece a paying customer for an Ottoman partner. An additional American ship would have faced a different wartime question: delivery to Greece as a neutral customer or retention through an American purchase. In the latter counterfactual, the US Navy would have acquired a ship outside its usual standard battleship pattern, with a speed of twenty-three knots.

evidence.note: A hypothetical American order alongside Salamis, exchange-rate and diplomatic motives, and alternative wartime delivery or American retention.

segments.summary: An American order alongside Salamis raises questions about price, procurement diplomacy and the fate of a neutral customer's ship in wartime.

segments.title: New Greek warships disrupted crews across the fleet
segments.body: New destroyers and Averof required crews while the Greek fleet was expanding. Filling those ships took men from existing vessels, spreading the disruption across the fleet. Greece nevertheless handled the transition well enough to establish an early reputation for action. Kountouriotis's aggressive reputation then influenced Ottoman decisions about naval operations.

evidence.note: New ships drew personnel from existing Greek crews, while successful early action and the admiral's aggressive reputation influenced Ottoman decisions.

segments.summary: Crewing Averof and new destroyers unsettled existing ships, but early Greek activity still established a reputation that influenced Ottoman planning.

segments.title: Could Constantinople have fallen during the First Balkan War?
segments.body: The counterfactual depends on Greece defeating the Ottoman fleet and forcing the Dardanelles despite the coastal guns. Bulgarian forces had already driven the opposing Ottoman army deep into Gallipoli, so a Greek breakthrough could have gained allied support on one bank of the straits. Greek sea power could then have cut off reinforcements reaching Constantinople from the Asian side while Bulgarian armies pressed from Europe. This combination might have made the city fall, although the Bulgarian rather than Greek army was geographically positioned to take it.

evidence.note: A possible Greek breakthrough against the straits guns, Bulgarian support on one bank, interruption of Asian reinforcements, and Bulgaria's proximity to Constantinople.

segments.summary: A stronger Greek fleet might have forced the straits while Bulgarian armies approached Constantinople, but the likely landward conqueror would still have been Bulgaria.
segments.question: With more Greek spending and more Ottoman corruption, could Constantinople have fallen in 1913?
segments.answerShort: Possibly: Greek control of the straits could have cut Ottoman reinforcement while Bulgarian armies closed on the city, making Bulgaria the likelier captor.

segments.title: What if Greece had bought Swiftsure and Triumph?
segments.body: Buying Swiftsure and Triumph in 1903 would have added substantial firepower to the Greek navy. It would also raise the question of whether Greece still acquired Georgios Averof. If all three ships were available, Greece would have had a very different fighting line. With Averof retained, the additional ships would have overwhelmed the Ottoman line much more decisively.

evidence.note: The proposed 1903 purchase would add Greek firepower, with the overwhelming advantage conditional on also acquiring Averof.

segments.summary: Adding Swiftsure and Triumph to a Greek line that still acquired Averof would have produced a much more powerful force against the Ottomans.
segments.question: How would Elli have changed if Greece had bought Swiftsure and Triumph in 1903?
segments.answerShort: If Greece also retained Averof, the two additional pre-dreadnoughts would have made its fighting line dramatically stronger than the Ottoman line.

segments.title: Could Anglo-French intervention have divided Ottoman territory earlier?
segments.body: An earlier division of Ottoman territory is a strong possibility in a scenario where commerce raiding brings Britain and France into the war and they judge intervention necessary. If Greece then held the Dardanelles and Bulgaria held Constantinople through World War I, there would be a secure route through the Black Sea to supply Russia. A battlecruiser escaping into the remaining Ottoman territory would face a different problem. In an eastern Mediterranean port, the Royal Navy could besiege her by waiting outside. If she entered the Black Sea, British ships could probably track her down and pursue her without the same fortifications holding them back. These outcomes depend on the Greek and Bulgarian territorial gains being retained into World War I.

evidence.note: Conditional support for an earlier Ottoman partition after Anglo-French intervention, followed by Russian supply through the Black Sea and alternative blockade or pursuit of a battlecruiser.

segments.summary: Intervention after Ottoman commerce raiding could have brought an earlier territorial division, with consequences for Russian supply and a battlecruiser's refuge during World War I.
segments.question: If Britain or France had joined the war because of commerce raiding, could the Ottoman Empire have been split up earlier?
segments.answerShort: Yes, that is a strong possibility if Britain and France judged intervention necessary. Greek and Bulgarian control of the straits could then have changed supply routes and naval operations in World War I.

segments.title: Would a victorious Bulgaria still join the Central Powers?
segments.body: A Bulgaria that reached Constantinople with British and French help would have had a strong reason to reconsider its later alliances. Its historical alignment with the Central Powers does not make the same choice inevitable in this counterfactual. An alliance would need to offer Bulgaria a realistic advantage. Bulgaria might have remained neutral or changed its alignment, with Italy providing the comparison.

evidence.note: British and French assistance changes Bulgaria's incentives, with neutrality or an Italian-style change of alignment proposed as alternatives.

segments.summary: A Bulgaria rewarded through British and French assistance in 1912-13 would have had less reason to enter World War I on the Central Powers' side.
segments.question: Would Bulgaria still have joined the Central Powers if it had gained more from the First Balkan War?
segments.answerShort: Its choice could have changed. Territorial gains enabled by British and French help would have given Bulgaria reasons to remain neutral or reconsider its alliances.

segments.title: What could the other Balkan navies contribute?
segments.body: Bulgaria did possess torpedo boats during the Balkan War. The relatively modern cruisers were among the Ottoman navy's strongest assets.

evidence.note: Bulgarian torpedo boats and the relative value of modern Ottoman cruisers.

segments.summary: Bulgaria possessed torpedo boats, while modern cruisers were among the Ottoman navy's strongest assets.
segments.question: How did the other nations' navies perform in the Balkan War, and did Bulgaria really have torpedo boats?
segments.answerShort: Bulgaria had torpedo boats, and modern cruisers were among the Ottoman navy's strongest assets.

segments.title: Why Elli and Lemnos had little influence on World War I
segments.body: Elli and Lemnos had little influence on naval thinking for World War I. Most navies did not expect to outrun opposing forces by such a margin. That limited how readily they could apply these battles to their own operations. David Beatty might have seen the possibility of conducting a similar naval operation.

evidence.note: Limited influence on other navies because they did not expect a comparable speed advantage, with Beatty suggested as a possible exception.

segments.summary: Most navies did not expect the speed advantage that made Elli and Lemnos possible, limiting their interest in copying the operations.
